entries.definition: Software that takes a goal and acts on it — running commands, editing files, browsing — usually by asking a language model what to do next. It is not the model, and it is not the sandbox; it runs inside the sandbox.
A machine that keeps running with no deadline and no idle sleep, so a message can arrive at any hour. It is three settings, not one, and the cost depends on what an idle hour bills.
A copy of the disk kept somewhere else, usually for disaster recovery. It is not a snapshot you can boot, and it rarely includes memory.
A save point inside one machine that you can rewind to, in place. boxd allows ten per machine; they die with the machine and cannot start a second one.
Starting a machine from its disk with nothing in memory. Files and installed software are there; processes that were running are not.
A process isolated by the host's shared kernel. Fast and light, and a weaker boundary than a VM: a kernel bug can cross it. Docker runs containers inside a machine.
A copy that shares unchanged data until one side writes. It is why a fork can appear in a second and use almost no extra disk until the copies diverge.
Network traffic leaving the machine. Some providers bill it per GB, some include an allowance, some do not bill it at all, and several publish no rate.

Usually a bundle of settings a new machine starts with — variables, secret files, repositories, credential switches. At Runtime the same word means a running sandbox. At Boat it is config, not an image.
A new machine copied from another. The copy may include memory and running processes or only the disk; the source may pause or keep running; the copy may be slightly stale.
A GiB is 1,073,741,824 bytes; a GB is 1,000,000,000. Providers mix them, so a 50 GB disk and 50 GiB of memory are about 7% apart. Runtime is explicit: GiB for memory, decimal GB for disk.
A coding-agent program such as Claude Code, Codex or OpenCode. Several providers preinstall several harnesses and let you prompt them by name; that is not the same as hosting the agent for you.
The layer that runs virtual machines and keeps them apart. KVM is Linux's; Firecracker and Cloud Hypervisor are small, fast hypervisors built on it.
A rule that parks a machine after a period without activity. What counts as activity varies: network traffic, data through a URL, a running command, or an open terminal.
A template a machine boots from: an OS plus installed software. Providers differ on whether you can bring your own, build one from a Dockerfile, or only pick from a catalogue.
Network traffic arriving at the machine. Usually free; the interesting question is who is allowed to send it.
The core of the operating system. “Own kernel” means a kernel bug inside your machine cannot directly reach anyone else's — the main reason VMs isolate better than containers.
A hard deadline after which the machine stops or is deleted, counted from creation or last resume rather than from activity. Distinct from an idle timer, and easy to confuse with it.
Model Context Protocol: a standard way to give an AI assistant tools. Several providers ship an MCP server so Claude or ChatGPT can create and drive sandboxes for you.
A virtual machine kept small and fast to start, still with its own kernel. Firecracker is the common implementation; it is the middle ground between a container and a full VM.
Parking a machine so it resumes quickly. The word says nothing about memory: check whether RAM survives, whether that is guaranteed, and what a paused hour costs.

A fake credential given to the machine while the real value stays outside it. An egress proxy swaps the real value in for requests to named hosts. It only works for the protocols and headers the proxy supports.
A monthly fee that converts into usage rather than being a fee on top. It is still a floor: a light month costs the plan price, and unused plan time usually expires.
A numbered door on a machine. A web server usually listens on 3000 or 8000; a database on 5432. Exposing a port means making that door reachable from outside.

Provisioned memory is what the machine is allowed to use; resident memory is what it is actually holding. Most providers bill the first; boxd bills the second, which makes the bill depend on your software.
A limit that refuses new work rather than charging for it. Sandboxer's stopped-storage quota is an example: over it, new sandboxes are refused until you delete something.
Full administrator rights inside the machine. Normal on a VM, and a reason a VM is a stronger boundary than a container running as an unprivileged user.
One isolated computer for one job, usually short-lived and usually reached over a network. Providers also call it an instance, a machine or a box.
A link with a time-limited token in it, so it works without an API key for a while. Convenient for opening a preview in a browser; it is a bearer credential until it expires.
A service-level agreement: a promised uptime with a remedy if it is missed. Several providers in this set publish none, and one publishes a promise its status page was not meeting during research.
A saved copy of a machine. It may include memory and processes or only the disk, may be restorable in place or only into a new machine, and may or may not let you choose an older one.
A ceiling that stops usage when reached. It is not money and does not add funds: Agent 37's per-instance budget and InstaBox's monthly cap are examples. Runtime's per-sandbox cap is a lifetime cap.
The standard way to get a shell on a remote Linux machine. Some providers offer it on a real port, some tunnel it, and one offers an interactive shell that is not SSH at all.
A starting image plus defaults. It can be a Dockerfile build, a named snapshot, or a fixed catalogue entry, and the difference decides whether you can carry your own setup forward.
A credential carried in the link itself. Anyone with the link is in, so it behaves like a password and leaks like one.
A disk you attach to a machine, separate from its root disk. Support varies from “four volumes per machine” to “no volumes at all”, and a volume often cannot be snapshotted or shared for writing.
Resuming a machine whose memory was kept, so processes continue instead of restarting. Fast, and usually the state that keeps billing for memory while parked.
